description: Standards for making digital content and products accessible to people with disabilities. Often referenced by public-sector accessibility regulation (EU Web Accessibility Directive, US Section 508, UK Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations).

issuing_bodies.name: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative
issuing_bodies.remit: Develops accessibility standards and techniques for the web.

issuing_bodies.name: International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission

standards.name: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2
standards.summary: Technical standard for web content accessibility. Organised under four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust (POUR). WCAG 2.2 adds nine success criteria over 2.1 including target size, dragging movements, consistent help, accessible authentication.
key_principles: Perceivable — alternatives for non-text content, captions, adaptability, distinguishable
Operable — keyboard accessible, enough time, no seizure-inducing content, navigable, input modalities
Robust — compatible with current and future user tools (including assistive tech)
referenced_in_regulation: UK Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018

standards.name: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 3.0 (draft)
standards.summary: Working draft; not a recommendation. Will cover a broader scope than WCAG 2.x including non-web content. Introduces a new outcome-based conformance model.

standards.name: Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines 2.0
standards.summary: Accessibility requirements for tools that produce web content (e.g. CMS, blog editors, design tools). Two parts: A — authoring tool UI is accessible; B — tool supports production of accessible content.
key_principles: Part A — authoring UI is accessible to disabled authors
Part B — tool supports authors in creating WCAG-conforming content

standards.name: Accessible Rich Internet Applications 1.2
standards.summary: Provides a framework for adding semantics to web applications (roles, states, properties) for assistive technologies. Not a replacement for native HTML semantics.
key_principles: Roles describe what a thing is
States describe what's happening right now
Use ARIA only when native HTML lacks the semantic
'No ARIA is better than bad ARIA'

standards.name: EN 301 549 — Accessibility requirements for ICT products and services
standards.summary: European harmonised accessibility standard covering ICT products and services. Incorporates WCAG requirements for web content and extends to hardware, software, documentation, and support services. Mandatory reference for EU public-sector procurement.
key_principles: Category-specific requirements (web, non-web software, hardware, documentation, support, two-way voice, video with audio)
Incorporates WCAG 2.1 AA (moving to 2.2) for web content
